item.title: The First Price Cut: How Long to Wait, and How Much
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Holding your price and waiting for the market to come to you sounds patient. In today's Flathead market, it usually just means a longer, more expensive path to the same number. Here's how to time and size the first cut instead.
item.content:encoded:
The First Price Cut: How Long to Wait, and How Much

Every seller gets the same advice when a listing goes quiet: give it more time. Don't panic. The right buyer is out there.

That advice isn't wrong, exactly. It's just incomplete, and in the current Kalispell and Whitefish market, incomplete advice gets expensive. The sellers I watch close nearest to their actual number aren't the ones who held their price the longest. They're the ones who moved once, early, and moved enough to matter.

Two Different Questions, One Bad Habit

"Should I cut my price?" isn't really one question. It's two — how long do I wait and how much do I cut — and most sellers answer both of them by feel instead of by evidence. They wait because waiting feels safer than admitting the number might be wrong. Then, when they finally move, they cut just enough to feel like they did something, which is usually the worst amount: too small to reach a new pool of buyers, too public not to signal that the house is struggling.

Treat them as two separate decisions, each with its own answer, and the whole process gets a lot less emotional.

How Long to Wait

The honest answer is shorter than most sellers want to hear, and it's shorter than it was a year ago. Earlier this week I wrote about Kalispell's median days on market stretching to 77, up from 62 a year ago (source: Movoto Kalispell market data, period through August 2026, page updated September 21, 2026). That number isn't just a market snapshot — it's the clock every listing is actually running against now, whether the seller has looked at it or not.

Here's what that means in practice: your first two to three weeks on market are the only period where you're seeing your true audience. Every buyer actively searching your price band and area sees a new listing in that window — saved searches fire, agents preview, the algorithm gives you its best push. That audience doesn't come back a second time with the same energy. If showings are thin and the ones you get don't return for a second look in that window, that's not a sign to wait longer. It's the answer.

Waiting past three weeks with no meaningful activity doesn't buy you more information — it buys you a listing that's aged into "still here" on a buyer's search, competing against houses that are new. At 77 days as the current median, a house that's already sitting at day 30 with no traction isn't halfway through a normal process. It's telling you something the calendar can't fix.

What a Too-Small Cut Actually Signals

This is where sellers lose the most value without realizing it. A five-thousand-dollar trim on a $650,000 listing doesn't reach a single new buyer — most search filters work in round increments, and a cut that doesn't cross one of those thresholds is invisible to anyone who isn't already watching your listing.

But it isn't invisible to the people who are watching. Agents tracking the MLS see a small reduction and read it correctly: a seller testing the water, expecting to cut again. Buyers who've already toured and passed see the same thing and wait, betting there's another cut coming before they need to act. A small first cut doesn't create urgency. It advertises that patience will be rewarded — which means the next offer you get, if one comes at all, tends to come in low, anchored to the number you'll probably drop to next.

The sellers who cut once and move on are the ones who size that first cut to actually change who sees the house, not just to move the number on the listing sheet.

Sizing the Cut Off Comparables, Not a Round Number

The fix isn't cutting bigger for the sake of it — it's cutting off the right information. Pull what's actually closed within roughly a mile in the last 60 to 90 days, not what's currently listed and not what a neighbor claims they were offered in conversation. Closings are evidence. Everything else is a guess dressed up as a data point.

Once you have that number, size your reduction to land your listing in front of a different search bracket entirely — below a round threshold buyers actually filter on, not a few thousand dollars under where you started. A house that moves from $749,000 to $739,000 hasn't changed who sees it. The same house moving to $725,000 has. One clean move that crosses a real line does more than three small ones that never do, and it costs you less in perception each time, because there's only one move to explain instead of a pattern to defend.

The Practical Version

If you're inside your first three weeks, watch traffic and second visits, not the calendar. If you're past that window with thin activity, the question isn't whether to move — it's how far, measured against what's actually closed nearby, not what feels fair. One deliberate cut, sized correctly and made early, beats three apologetic ones every time.

So here's the question worth sitting with if your listing has gone quiet: are you waiting because the data says wait, or because moving the number feels like admitting something you'd rather not?

item.title: Elk Camp and Closing Dates: What Hunting Season Does to a Flathead Calendar
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Archery season opened September 5 and backcountry rifle districts are already in. Here's what that actually does to inspections, showings, and closing dates across the Flathead Valley right now.
item.content:encoded:
Elk Camp and Closing Dates: What Hunting Season Does to a Flathead Calendar

Archery season opened September 5. A handful of backcountry districts — 150, 280, and 316 — are already into their general rifle season, weeks ahead of the statewide rifle opener on October 24. If you're buying or selling in the Flathead Valley right now, that's not background noise. For a real share of the people on both sides of a transaction, the next several weeks run on a hunting calendar as much as a closing calendar, whether their agent has noticed or not.

I hunt this valley myself, so this isn't a lifestyle piece written from the outside looking in. It's the same discipline I brought to scheduling movements and coordinating with people who weren't always reachable — applied to something lower-stakes, but with the same basic problem: if you build a plan assuming everyone's phone works and everyone's available "whenever," that plan breaks the first time it meets reality.

Where This Shows Up First: Showings

A listing agent who sets a showing window without asking about hunting plans is going to eat a few no-shows this month, and more in October. It's not that buyers and sellers are being difficult — it's that "available anytime" quietly stops being true for a meaningful slice of the valley starting in September and doesn't fully reset until well into November.

The fix is simple and it's the same one I use for anything with a hard deadline: ask early, and ask specifically. Not "are you around this month," but "are there dates you're out of cell range, and dates you know you're back." A seller who tells you October 24–28 is elk camp isn't giving you a scheduling headache — they're giving you the information that keeps a showing from getting booked into a week that was never going to work.

Where It Actually Bites: Inspections and Walkthroughs

Showings are an inconvenience if you get the timing wrong. Inspections and final walkthroughs are different — they sit on a contract with dates attached, and Montana purchase agreements don't pause for opening weekend.

If a buyer or seller is going to be in the backcountry during an inspection contingency window, that needs to be flagged before the offer is written, not discovered three days before the deadline. The same goes for a final walkthrough scheduled against a closing date — if the seller who needs to be present is going to be miles from a cell tower, that's a conversation for the purchase agreement's timeline, not a last-minute scramble with a title company waiting on a signature.

None of this is complicated. It just has to happen on purpose. I build every closing calendar around the assumption that at least one person involved — buyer, seller, sometimes both — has a week where they're genuinely unreachable, and I plan the contingency deadlines and walkthrough dates around that instead of hoping it doesn't come up.

What a Realistic October Looks Like

By the time the statewide rifle opener hits on October 24, this stops being a background consideration and becomes the default assumption. Multiple-day gaps in availability. Weekends that are off the table months in advance. Sellers who want their home shown by appointment only, with real notice, because they're not going to drop everything for a same-day request during the two weeks that matter most to them all year.

None of that has to slow a transaction down. It just means the calendar gets built with those weeks already blocked out, instead of getting rebuilt around them after a missed deadline. A seller who tells me in September which weeks in October are off-limits gets a listing strategy and a showing plan that respects that from day one. A buyer who flags the same thing gets an offer timeline that doesn't assume they're glued to their phone during opening weekend.

The Practical Version

If you're planning to list, buy, or are already under contract heading into archery or rifle season: say so, early, and say so specifically. Give dates, not "sometime in October." If you're working with an agent who hasn't asked, ask them how they plan around it — the answer tells you a lot about whether your calendar is going to hold up once the valley empties out for a few weeks.

This isn't about slowing anything down. It's about building the plan around the parts of your life that don't move for a closing date, instead of finding out the hard way that they don't.

Do you have dates this fall where you know you'll be out of range — and does your current plan already account for them, or is it going to find out the hard way?

item.title: The Sibling Buyout: How Heirs Actually Price One Person Keeping the House
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: When one sibling wants to keep an inherited Flathead Valley home and the others want their share, the disagreement almost always starts with the number. Here's how that number actually gets set — and where buyouts go wrong.
item.content:encoded:
The Sibling Buyout: How Heirs Actually Price One Person Keeping the House

Three siblings inherit their parents' house in the Flathead Valley. Two are ready to sell. One wants to stay — maybe they've been the one checking on the place, maybe it's just home. Everyone agrees, in principle, that a buyout is the fair answer.

Then someone asks the question that actually matters: bought out at what price? And that's where the agreement usually stops.

If you're the personal representative or one of the heirs trying to work this out, here's how that number gets set in practice, and the places this quietly falls apart.

First, the disclaimer that has to come first: I'm a real estate agent, not an attorney or a CPA. Montana probate has its own rules about distribution, timing, and what a personal representative needs court approval to do, and those rules depend on the will and the specifics of the estate. What follows is meant to sharpen the questions you bring to your attorney and CPA, not to replace their answers.

Whose number counts, and whose doesn't

Every sibling buyout I've seen struggle started with the same mistake: someone's opinion of value got treated as the value.

The sibling who wants to keep the house has every incentive to think it's worth less. The siblings being bought out have every incentive to think it's worth more. The county assessor's number reflects tax policy, not market value, and is often years behind. A sibling's memory of "what the Petersons got for their place down the road" isn't a comparable, it's a rumor.

None of those numbers can settle a disagreement, because none of them are neutral. The fix is the same one that works in every estate sale: an independent, licensed appraisal — often the same date-of-death appraisal the estate needs for tax purposes anyway. It isn't a perfect substitute for what the house would fetch on the open market, but it's defensible, it's in writing, and it's nobody's opinion. Get it before anyone states a number out loud. Positions harden fast once a figure is on the table, even an informal one.

How the buying sibling actually pays for it

Once there's a value, the next fight is usually about how the buyout gets financed — and this is where I see families lose months.

The sibling keeping the house typically needs to refinance the inherited property into a new mortgage in their own name, using the loan proceeds to pay the other heirs their share. That means qualifying on their own income and their own debts, with a fresh appraisal from a lender who has zero interest in the estate's peace and quiet. A number the family agreed on informally can come in lower — or higher — once a bank's appraiser looks at the same house. Confirm financing capacity in week one, not after everyone has emotionally settled on a figure. I've watched a sibling agree to "buy the others out," spend two months telling the family it was handled, and then fail to qualify for the loan — which restarts the entire negotiation from a much angrier starting point.

The costs that don't exist in a normal sale

A sibling buyout isn't a normal purchase, and pricing it like one skips real costs that need to be assigned somewhere.

There's no listing agent commission, but there's often a new appraisal fee, refinance closing costs, title work, and sometimes a small transfer or recording cost depending on how the deed moves. Someone has to decide whether those come off the top of the buyout price, get split evenly among all heirs, or land entirely on the sibling keeping the house. There's no universal answer — it's a negotiation — but it needs to be decided explicitly and in writing, not assumed. The estates that avoid resentment later are the ones where this got settled before the closing, not argued about after.

When the appraisal comes in lower than someone expected

This happens more than families expect, and it's worth planning for before it does. If the independent appraisal lands below what a sibling was counting on, the instinct is to argue the number. Resist that. The more useful conversation is what the family does with the number: does the buyout proceed at the appraised value, does the family get a second opinion, does the sibling staying in the house need to bring cash to the table to make the others whole. Decide the process for handling a disappointing number before you have one — it's a much calmer conversation in the abstract than it is once a specific figure is sitting in front of everyone.

Probate puts a clock on all of this

Montana probate timelines add real pressure here that a normal home sale doesn't have. Depending on the type of probate and the estate's obligations, there can be deadlines for distributing assets or closing out the estate that don't wait for siblings to reach comfortable consensus on financing. That's exactly why I push families to get the appraisal and the financing conversation moving in parallel, early, rather than sequentially — waiting for one before starting the other is often what turns a manageable few months into a year.

So here's the question worth asking before the next family conversation: has anyone actually gotten an independent number yet, or is everyone still negotiating from a guess?

If you're navigating a sibling buyout or an estate sale anywhere in the Flathead Valley, I'm glad to walk through the real estate side of it while your attorney and CPA handle the law and the tax basis. item.title: Insurance First, Offer Second: What Flathead Buyers Skip Until It's Too Late
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Most Flathead Valley buyers call an insurance carrier the week before closing. Here's why calling before you write an offer protects your deal instead.
item.content:encoded:
Insurance First, Offer Second: What Flathead Buyers Skip Until It's Too Late

If you're house-hunting in Kalispell or Whitefish right now, you've probably spent real hours comparing floor plans, mudroom storage, and which elementary school a property feeds into. Here's a question that matters just as much and gets asked far too late: have you called an insurance carrier about this specific property yet?

Most buyers haven't. Most buyers call for the first time the week before closing — sometimes after the offer is already signed, sometimes after the lender has already asked for proof of coverage and started the clock ticking. By then, a bad quote isn't a data point. It's a problem sitting on top of your closing date.

Why This Gets Skipped

It's not that buyers don't care about insurance. It's that insurance doesn't feel urgent during the search phase. You're focused on whether the house works for your life — the number of bedrooms, the commute, whether the shop has 220V. Insurance feels like paperwork you'll deal with later, the same category as picking a title company or scheduling movers.

The problem is that in the Flathead Valley, insurance isn't always paperwork. On certain properties, it's a gatekeeper.

What Actually Moves a Quote Here

A lot of Flathead Valley inventory sits in or near the wildland-urban interface — timbered lots, homes backed up to national forest, properties out toward Foys Lake, Herron Park, or the benches above Whitefish where the tree line comes right up to the house. Carriers underwrite those properties differently than they underwrite a flat lot in town, and a few specific things drive the number:

Roof age and material. A 20-year-old roof, or a wood-shake roof anywhere near timber, is one of the fastest ways to get a declined quote rather than just an expensive one. Some carriers won't write wildfire-zone coverage on wood shake at any price. If a listing photo shows shake shingles and you're picturing it as a future re-roof project, that project may need to happen before closing, not after.

Defensible space. Carriers increasingly ask about the buffer between the structure and the nearest trees or brush — sometimes with a formula, sometimes with an inspector or a satellite-imagery review. A beautifully wooded lot that reads as private and quiet to you can read as high-risk to an underwriter if the canopy comes within a few feet of the eaves.

Water source, for rural properties. Homes on well and septic, especially without a fire hydrant within a set distance, get asked about static water sources — a pond, a cistern, proximity to a creek. It's not a question most buyers expect, and it's not one most listing agents volunteer.

Prior claims history on the property, not just on you. A house with a claims history the seller didn't necessarily disclose can affect your quote regardless of your own record.

Any one of these can turn a routine quote into a declined one, a high-deductible one, or a "we can write it, but not at the number you budgeted" one.

Why This Belongs on the Pre-Offer List

Here's the sequence that causes trouble: buyer falls for a property, writes an offer, offer gets accepted, buyer finally calls for insurance during the option period or right before closing, and the quote comes back either unaffordable or the carrier declines to write it altogether. Now the buyer is scrambling for a second or third carrier with a closing date already on the calendar and a lender who needs proof of coverage to fund. That pressure rarely produces a better outcome — it produces whatever policy is available in time, at whatever price.

Compare that to calling a carrier — or better, two or three — before you write the offer. You're not committing to anything. You're gathering the one piece of information that can quietly kill a deal a home inspection would never catch, because a home inspector checks whether the roof leaks, not whether an insurance company will cover it. Ten minutes on the phone with a local agent who knows Flathead County underwriting, using the listing's address and rough details, tells you what you're walking into before you're financially attached to the outcome.

This isn't about being pessimistic on a home you're excited about. It's about protecting the offer you're about to make — treating insurance as due diligence with the same seriousness you'd give well flow or septic inspection, not as a closing-week formality.

The Practical Version

Before you write on a property in a wooded or rural setting: get a preliminary quote or at least a same-day phone read from a local carrier. Ask directly about roof material and age, defensible space requirements, and water source if it's on well. If a property is going to be hard to insure, you want that answer during your due-diligence window — when it still has leverage in the negotiation, or a walk-away option attached to it — not after you've waived contingencies.

This article covers general practice and is not insurance or legal advice — coverage availability and underwriting requirements vary by carrier and change over time; confirm specifics with a licensed insurance agent before writing an offer.

If you're looking at a property in the wildland-urban interface and want to know what questions to ask before you write — or you've already got a quote back that has you second-guessing the deal — what would it change to have that conversation this week instead of during your closing-week scramble?

item.title: The Buyout Loan: Why Refinancing to Keep the House Is Harder Than It Sounds
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: "I'll just refinance and keep the house" is the plan almost every spouse floats first in a Montana divorce — and the one that falls apart the most. Here's the sequence a buyout refinance actually requires, step by step.
item.content:encoded:
The Buyout Loan: Why Refinancing to Keep the House Is Harder Than It Sounds

If you've said the words "I'll just refinance and keep the house" out loud to your attorney, you're not alone. It's the first plan almost every spouse floats in a Flathead Valley divorce. It's also, more often than any other plan, the one that quietly falls apart three months later — not because anyone changed their mind, but because nobody walked through what a buyout refinance actually requires before it got written into the settlement.

This isn't legal or tax advice, and it isn't a case for keeping the house or selling it. Your attorney and your lender own those numbers. What follows is the sequence — the steps a buyout refinance has to clear, in order, and where each one tends to snag.

You're qualifying alone now, on one income

The mortgage on the house was likely approved on two incomes and two sets of debts. A buyout refinance has to qualify on one of each. That sounds obvious stated plainly, but it's the step most people haven't priced out before it's in the settlement agreement — a debt-to-income ratio that worked fine for a household of two can miss the mark for a household of one, especially once spousal support, if any, is added to the liability side of that math rather than the income side, or not counted as income at all depending on how long it's guaranteed to continue. The lender runs this number. It doesn't care what the decree says should happen — only whether the person keeping the house can actually carry the loan alone.

The appraisal doesn't know what number is in the settlement

Somewhere in the settlement conversation, a home value got agreed to — sometimes from a comparative market analysis, sometimes from a number one spouse remembered from three years ago, sometimes from what felt fair. The refinance doesn't use that number. It uses a fresh appraisal, ordered fresh, valuing the house as of today.

If that appraisal comes in lower than the figure written into the settlement, the equity the other spouse is owed doesn't shrink to match — but the amount available to refinance against does. That gap has to be closed with cash, a renegotiated split, or a different plan entirely, and it's a far better conversation to have before the settlement is signed than after the appraisal report lands.

The spouse being bought out is still on the loan — and the liability — until closing actually happens

This is the one that catches people off guard. A settlement agreement can say the house belongs to one spouse and the other is being bought out. That agreement does not remove either name from the existing mortgage. Only the new loan closing does that. Until the refinance actually funds, both spouses remain contractually liable for the original mortgage, whatever the decree says about who's responsible for what. A late payment during that window shows up on both credit reports. "The divorce is final" and "the refinance closed" are two different dates, and the gap between them is where risk sits for the spouse who's supposed to be out.

Timing the closing against a deadline that doesn't move for a lender

Settlement agreements often include a date: refinance and remove the other spouse's name by such-and-such, or the house gets listed instead. Lenders don't work around court deadlines — they work through underwriting timelines, appraisal scheduling, and title work, the same as any other refinance. Building a 30-day cushion between the loan's realistic closing date and the settlement's deadline isn't overcautious. It's the difference between a clean transition and a scramble that lands back in front of the judge.

When the refinancing spouse can't qualify for the full amount

Sometimes the numbers simply don't work — income doesn't support the loan amount needed to pay out the other spouse's share, even with the house's full equity behind it. This isn't a failure, and it isn't a dead end. It's information, and it usually means one of a few paths: a smaller buyout paired with a payment plan for the remainder, a co-signer, a longer runway before refinancing is attempted again, or — for some couples — selling the house and splitting the proceeds turns out to be the cleaner outcome for both people once the refinance math is actually run rather than assumed.

A question worth asking before it's in writing

If your settlement includes a buyout refinance, has anyone actually run the numbers — income, appraisal, timeline — or is the plan resting on what felt fair in a conversation?

That's not a question your attorney can answer alone, and it's not one I can answer instead of a lender. But it's the question worth asking before the number goes into the agreement, not after.

item.title: 62 to 77: What the Extra Two Weeks on Market Costs Flathead Sellers
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Kalispell's median days on market has stretched from 62 a year ago to 77 today. Here's what that extra two weeks actually costs a seller, and what to do about it this week instead of waiting for spring.
item.content:encoded:
Sixty-two. Seventy-seven.

Those are Kalispell's median days on market a year ago and today, respectively (source: Movoto Kalispell, MT market data, period through August 2026, page updated September 21, 2026). Fifteen extra days doesn't sound dramatic until you sit with what actually happens inside those two weeks — and it's worth sitting with, because a lot of sellers on the sidelines right now are measuring the wrong number entirely.

The Numbers First

Kalispell, current snapshot: median sale price $699,000, 693 active listings, median days on market 77 — up from 62 a year ago (source: Movoto, data through August 2026, updated September 21, 2026).

On rate, the Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey put the 30-year fixed at 6.95% for the week of September 17, 2026, up from 6.76% the week before (source: Freddie Mac PMMS).

That's the whole picture in two sentences. Everything below is what a seller actually does with it.

What "Two Extra Weeks" Really Means

A house that used to find a buyer in about nine weeks now takes closer to eleven. On paper that reads like a rounding error. In practice, those fifteen days are rarely quiet ones.

They're the window where a listing crosses from "new and interesting" to "still here" in a buyer's saved-search feed. They're the stretch where an agent previewing for a client starts asking why it hasn't sold yet, before ever asking what it's worth. And more often than not, they're the days where a price reduction gets discussed — not because the house changed, but because the calendar did.

Fifteen days by itself won't sink a listing. What sinks a listing is a seller who doesn't know those fifteen days are now the baseline, and who reads every one of them as evidence something is wrong with the house instead of evidence the whole market shifted underneath it.

The Mistake: Measuring Against Last Year

The seller who gets hurt in this market isn't the one who's slow to sell. It's the one comparing this listing to a house that sold in June of last year, in nine weeks, at full price — and quietly deciding their own house is underperforming when it's actually tracking right at this year's median.

That comparison is the trap. Sixty-two days was last year's market. Seventy-seven is this one. A house sitting at day 60 today isn't behind schedule. It's roughly on pace. The seller who doesn't know that will start second-guessing the price around week seven, right when patience was the correct answer.

The fix isn't complicated: know the current median before you list, not the one you remember from a friend's sale eighteen months ago.

What a Longer Market Actually Changes

A slower median doesn't just mean more waiting. It changes the mechanics of the deal itself, in three specific ways worth planning for before you're in the middle of them:

More price reductions happen before contract, not after listing. With more inventory for buyers to compare against, a house that opens a touch high has more competition sitting right next to it on the same search page. The reduction that used to be rare is now closer to routine — plan for the possibility rather than treating it as a failure if it happens.

Appraisal-gap language gets softer. When homes were moving in nine weeks, buyers waived contingencies to win multiple-offer situations. At 77 days, multiple offers are less common, and buyers have more room to ask for an appraisal contingency rather than bridging a gap in cash. Sellers should expect more negotiation on that clause, not less.

Buyers have more to compare you against. Six hundred ninety-three active listings means a buyer touring your house toured, or at least screened, several others this week. The house that shows clean, prices realistically against current comparables, and photographs well in the light it actually has is the one that doesn't need the full 77 days to find its buyer.

What This Means for You This Week

If you're already on the market and past day 60, don't panic — check your pace against 77, the current number, not 62. If you're inside that window, you're not behind. If you're well past it, that's the moment for an honest look at price against what's actually closed nearby in the last 30 days, not what's still asking.

If you're waiting for spring hoping the market "comes back" to last year's pace, ask yourself what specifically you think changes between now and April. Rates aren't the lever — they've moved up, not down, over the past two weeks, and a rate drop would bring more buyers into every listing at once, not just yours. The seller who prices correctly and lists into a quieter fall often does better than the one who waits for a crowded spring.

So here's the actual question worth asking this week: do you know what your house is worth against what's closed in the last 30 days — not what's currently asking, what closed — or are you still pricing off a market that expired sometime last year?

item.title: When the Right Advice Is \"Don't\"
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Why a Flathead Valley agent whose income depends on a closing sometimes has to argue against one — and why the clients who hear it are the ones who send people.
item.content:encoded:
When the Right Advice Is "Don't"

When was the last time someone in a commission-based job told you not to do the thing that pays them?

It doesn't come up much, because it isn't supposed to. The incentive in this business runs one direction: a transaction closes, or it doesn't, and only one of those outcomes puts money in an agent's pocket. So the harder conversations this month — the ones about planning a sale around a divorce timeline, sequencing an estate through probate, reading an offer past the headline number — have all assumed the client and the agent want the same thing: to get to closing, cleanly. This one is about what happens when they don't.

The Job Nobody Puts on the Business Card

Most of real estate is exactly what it looks like — pricing, marketing, negotiating, managing a timeline. But underneath that is a smaller, less comfortable job: telling a client that the deal sitting in front of them, the one they've already started picturing themselves living in or hoping to fund with, isn't the one to do. Not because the paperwork is wrong. Because the fit is.

That instinct isn't new to real estate for me. Years spent making calls where the cost of being wrong was measured in more than money teaches you a specific discipline: separate what you want to be true from what the situation is actually telling you, say the uncomfortable thing early, and let the decision-maker decide with full information rather than a comfortable version of it. Applied here, that means an agent's job isn't just to get a client to the table. It's to tell them, plainly, when the table isn't worth sitting at.

Three Situations, Told Without Names

None of what follows is one specific client — these are composites, built from patterns that show up often enough to be worth writing down.

The house that checks every box except one. A buyer finds a place with the right bedroom count, the right school district, the right price, and a driveway that turns into a sheet of ice every winter because of how the lot sits relative to the sun. On a July showing, nobody notices. The box-checking is satisfying enough that the one real problem gets waved off as something to "figure out later." Later, for a lot of buyers, means a house they resent by February. Pointing that out before the offer goes in doesn't kill every deal like it — some buyers hear it and go forward anyway, eyes open, which is a fine outcome. But they heard it first.

The offer that should be countered, not accepted. A seller gets a number that's close enough to asking that the temptation is to just take it and be done — especially after a slower stretch on the market. Sometimes that instinct is right. Sometimes the offer is soft in a way the headline price hides: a long due-diligence period, financing that hasn't been verified past a form letter, a closing date that doesn't actually work for the seller's own next move. Accepting fast isn't the same as accepting well, and a seller who's tired of waiting is exactly the seller who needs someone to slow the moment down for thirty seconds before signing.

The purchase that pencils out and shouldn't be stretched for. A buyer can technically qualify for a number that leaves almost nothing left over once the mortgage, taxes, insurance, and the realities of an older home are all sitting on the same monthly statement. The math works on paper. It's the kind of math that works right up until a furnace fails in January or a job gets shakier than expected. Telling a buyer that qualifying for a number isn't the same as being able to live inside it comfortably is not the advice that gets an offer written today. It's usually the advice that keeps someone in their house five years from now.

What It Actually Costs to Say No

Arguing against a transaction is not free for the person doing it. It costs a commission that might not come back around, at least not from that specific deal. It sometimes costs a client relationship if the advice lands wrong or the client wasn't ready to hear it. And it never comes with a thank-you in the moment — nobody feels grateful for being told to wait, or to pass, or to counter instead of just taking the win.

What it buys instead is longer and quieter: a client who, three years later, is still glad they didn't buy that house, or that they held out for a real offer instead of the first one. Those are the clients who refer people. Not because the transaction was exciting, but because someone was willing to be the person in the room whose job wasn't just to get the deal done.

What This Actually Sounds Like

It's rarely dramatic. It sounds like "before you write this offer, let's talk about what the driveway does every winter." It sounds like "I'd counter this, and here's specifically why." It sounds like "you qualify for this, and I want to make sure you also want to live inside it." None of it is a war story. It's a standard, applied the same way whether the deal is easy or hard: say the true thing before the offer is signed, not after.

If you're in the middle of a decision right now and something about it doesn't sit right — even if you can't quite name what — that instinct is worth a conversation before it's worth an offer.

item.title: Reading an Offer: What Sellers Look At After the Price
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: How Kalispell and Whitefish sellers compare competing offers on financing, earnest money, inspection terms, and closing timeline — not just the highest number on the page.
item.content:encoded:
Reading an Offer: What Sellers Look At After the Price

Two offers land on the same Kalispell listing within a day of each other. One is $18,000 higher. Most sellers open that one first, mentally accept it, and only skim the second. By the time the higher offer starts wobbling — a financing contingency that's tighter than it looked, an inspection window wide enough to renegotiate the price twice — the decision has usually already been made, and unwinding it costs weeks.

If you've ever wondered why a listing "in escrow" quietly reappears on the market a month later, this is usually why. The highest number on the page loses to a cleaner offer more often than sellers expect. Here's what actually determines whether an offer closes, in the order it's worth looking at.

Financing Type and What a Preapproval Letter Actually Promises

A cash offer and a conventional loan offer aren't the same offer even at an identical price — cash removes appraisal risk and loan-underwriting risk entirely. Below that, a preapproval letter is not a guarantee; it's a lender's statement that a buyer looked qualified on the information given at the time. Ask who issued it — a national call-center lender and a local Flathead Valley lender don't carry the same weight with a listing agent who's watched deals from both fall apart or sail through. A preapproval that's more than 60–90 days old, or one with unusually broad conditions, is worth a phone call to the loan officer before you get attached to that number.

Earnest Money as a Measure of Commitment

Earnest money isn't a fee — it's the buyer's skin in the game, and the size of it tells you something the purchase price doesn't. A token earnest deposit on a $650,000 Whitefish home is a signal, whether or not the buyer means it that way. Larger earnest money, especially with shorter contingency-removal deadlines attached to it, tends to come from buyers who've already decided this is the house. It also matters for what happens if the deal falls apart — what's refundable, what isn't, and under which contingencies, which is a conversation for your listing agent and the purchase agreement, not a guess.

Inspection Window and Appraisal-Gap Language

A long, open-ended inspection period is where an accepted offer quietly turns into a second round of price negotiation two weeks later. A shorter, clearly scoped window — or an as-is offer with a defined inspection-for-information-only clause — tells you the buyer isn't planning to use inspection as a re-trade tool. Appraisal-gap language matters more in a market where values have softened: a buyer who's committed to covering some or all of a gap between contract price and a low appraisal is worth materially more than one who hasn't addressed it at all, even at a slightly lower offer price.

Closing Date, Rent-Back Requests, and Who's Asking for What

Run the closing date against your own next move, not just the calendar. A 30-day close that leaves you scrambling for temporary housing can cost more in stress and moving expense than the $10,000 you gained on price. If a buyer is asking for a rent-back after closing so they can finish their own move, that's a negotiable point, not a red flag — but it needs terms in writing: daily rate, duration, and what happens if you're not out on schedule. Requests for seller-paid closing costs should be read against the net number, not the sticker price — a buyer asking for $8,000 in closing cost credit on top of a strong offer may still net you more than a lower, cleaner-looking number that carries no requests at all.

Comparing Two Offers Side by Side

Build a simple table before you decide anything: price, financing type and lender, earnest money amount and refundability, inspection window length, appraisal-gap terms, closing date against your own timeline, and any credits or rent-back requests. Laid out that way, the "obvious" choice is often less obvious than the headline price made it look. This is also where a buyer's own home-sale contingency belongs on the list — a buyer whose purchase depends on their current house selling first is carrying risk that a same-price, contingency-free offer isn't.

None of this replaces your listing agent walking the actual contract language with you line by line — financing conditions, contingency deadlines, and gap-coverage clauses should be confirmed against the specific purchase agreement in front of you, not a general framework.

If you're comparing offers right now, or getting ready to list and want to know what a strong offer looks like in this market before the first one arrives, that's exactly the kind of conversation worth having early.

item.title: Larch Season: The Two Weeks the Valley Turns Gold
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Western larch drops its needles instead of keeping them, and for a short window each fall the drainages around the Flathead go gold. Where it happens, roughly when it peaks, and why the timing shifts with elevation.
item.content:encoded:
Larch Season: The Two Weeks the Valley Turns Gold

Most people move to the Flathead for the summers. A fair number of them decide to stay because of two weeks in the fall they never saw coming.

Western larch — locals call it tamarack — is a conifer that does something conifers aren't supposed to do: it drops its needles. Every other evergreen on the mountainside holds green through the winter. The larch turns gold first, then rust, then bare, and for a short stretch every year whole drainages around this valley light up in a way that catches newcomers completely off guard. Nobody tells them to look up. They find out by accident, usually driving somewhere else.

Here's what that window actually looks like, where to see it, and what it has to do with whether you'd actually want to live here.

What You're Looking At

A larch isn't dying when it turns — it's doing what it does every single year. The needles go through a genuine color change: green to a soft yellow, then a deeper gold, then almost orange-rust right before they let go entirely. Because larch tends to grow in dense stands mixed among the true evergreens, the effect isn't one tree turning color — it's whole hillsides of gold set against the dark green of the Douglas fir and lodgepole that never change at all. From a distance it reads less like fall foliage and more like the mountain got lit from inside.

It's a different kind of color season than what most people picture when they think "autumn in the mountains." There's no red, almost no orange until the very end, and it doesn't happen on a deciduous tree in a yard — it happens on a conifer, on a slope, at a distance. That's exactly why it surprises people who moved here expecting Vermont and got something else entirely.

When It Peaks — and Why the Window Moves

The honest answer is that there isn't one fixed date, because elevation runs the calendar here more than the calendar does. Higher stands typically turn first, working down toward the valley floor as the weeks go on, which is why the color seems to migrate downhill through the season instead of happening everywhere at once. In a typical year that means the change gets underway in the second half of September at elevation and builds toward a broader, valley-wide peak sometime in the back half of October, occasionally stretching toward the start of November in a mild year. An early hard frost can compress the whole window; a warm, dry stretch can stretch it out. The only reliable rule is to watch the higher drainages first — if they're turning, the lower country is a couple of weeks behind.

Where to Go Look

You don't need a permit or a plan, just a direction to point the truck.

The Hungry Horse Reservoir area, up the South Fork past Columbia Falls, is some of the most reliable tamarack country in the valley — dense stands, big water, and far fewer people on a random Tuesday than Flathead Lake sees on a summer Saturday. The Middle Fork of the Flathead, where it runs alongside US-2 toward Glacier's southern boundary, puts you in larch country with almost no effort — it's a highway view, not a hike. For something closer to town, Herron Park on Kalispell's edge and the Rails to Trails corridor give you the color on a lunchtime walk. Further out, the Seeley-Swan valley and the North Fork Road toward Polebridge both run through heavy larch country, though the North Fork is unpaved and washboarded by this time of year — worth the trip, not worth doing on a schedule.

None of this requires Glacier Park itself, though the park's lower-elevation corridors carry their share of larch too, especially along the Middle Fork side. If you're headed that way, plan around the season change: the alpine section of Going-to-the-Sun Road closes with the first serious snow, typically before larch season fully wraps up, so check conditions before you commit a whole day to it.

What It Has to Do With Buying a House Here

I bring this up every fall for the same reason: it's the season that tells you whether you actually like it here, or just liked visiting in July.

A house that gets shown in June photographs beautifully and tells you almost nothing about what the property feels like the other nine months of the year. Larch season is a decent stand-in test. If you can picture yourself driving up the South Fork on a random Tuesday afternoon just to see the color change — not because you have to, just because you want to — that's a different kind of buyer than someone who's only ever pictured the dock in August. Both are fine reasons to be here. They just point toward different parts of the valley, and toward a very different conversation about what you're actually buying.

This isn't a pitch to buy in October. It's a suggestion: if you're seriously weighing a move to the Flathead, come back and drive it once the green thins out. The place you fall for in a fall storm of gold needles is the same one you'll be living in come February — and it's worth knowing which version you actually signed up for.

item.title: The Empty House in Winter: Protecting an Inherited Home Until It Sells
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Probate runs longer than the season does. What a family needs handled before the first hard freeze so an inherited Flathead home doesn't lose real money sitting vacant.
item.content:encoded:
The Empty House in Winter: Protecting an Inherited Home Until It Sells

Probate has its own calendar, and it rarely lines up with the one on the wall.

By the time an estate clears the paperwork, secures the personal representative's authority, and gets a house ready to list, it's not unusual for a Flathead property to sit empty through its first winter with nobody living in it. Nobody plans for that. It just happens — the legal side takes the time it takes, and the house sits there in the meantime, unattended, while temperatures do what they do in this valley from November through March.

An empty house doesn't fail all at once. It fails quietly, in ways nobody notices until spring, when the family walks in for a showing and finds out what a Flathead winter did to a place with no one watching it.

If you're a personal representative or an heir looking at a vacant house and a first freeze on the calendar, here's what actually needs handling — the practical care of an asset the family is holding on someone else's behalf, not the legal side, which is your attorney's to walk you through.

Call the insurer before you call anyone else

This is the one people skip, and it's the one that costs the most when they do.

A standard homeowners policy is written for an occupied house. Most carriers have a vacancy clause that limits or excludes coverage — water damage in particular — once a home sits empty past a stated number of consecutive days, often 30 to 60 depending on the policy. If a pipe freezes and bursts in an unoccupied house and the insurer can show the vacancy exclusion applied, the estate can be looking at a claim that pays little or nothing on exactly the kind of loss an empty winter house is most exposed to.

Tell the carrier the home is vacant, in writing, the day it becomes vacant. Ask directly whether the existing policy still covers it, whether a vacant-home endorsement or a separate vacant-property policy is needed, and what conditions that coverage requires — a working heat source above a minimum temperature is a common one. This is a conversation for the estate's attorney and the insurer, not a guess on my end, but it needs to happen before the first hard freeze, not after a claim.

Heat, water, and the pipes in between

Once coverage is sorted, the mechanical decision is heat left on versus the system drained. Both work; picking neither is what causes damage.

Left occupied-style, most guidance is to keep the thermostat no lower than the mid-50s, which keeps interior wall cavities above freezing without running a full heating bill on an empty house. The alternative is a full drain-down: water shut off at the main, lines blown out or drained, and antifreeze in traps and toilets — done properly, usually by a plumber, so nothing gets missed. A house that's heated but has water shut off and lines drained anyway is the safest combination, since a frozen pipe with no water behind it does far less damage than one that's pressurized.

Either way, pay attention to the pipes on exterior walls and in unheated spaces — garages, crawl spaces, an addition with thinner insulation — since those freeze first regardless of what the thermostat says. And don't forget the water heater; draining it or leaving it running is its own decision, not an afterthought to the rest of the system.

Snow, ice, and a house that doesn't look empty

An inherited home still needs a driveway a plow can reach and a roofline that isn't building an ice dam over the gutters. Arrange snow removal on a standing schedule, not a call-when-someone-remembers basis — both so the house stays passable for showings once it's ready to list, and because an unplowed drive and an unshoveled walk are the fastest visual signal to a passerby that nobody's home.

Ice damming is worth a specific mention: heat escaping through an under-insulated attic melts snow on the roof, it refreezes at the colder eave, and water backs up under the shingles into the house. It's a slow, expensive kind of damage that shows up as a stain on a ceiling months later. A quick check of attic insulation and gutter clearing before the snow starts is cheap compared to what a winter of damming can do.

A set of eyes, on a schedule

Mail piling up in a box, a light that's never on, snow that never gets tracked — these are the details that tell the wrong kind of visitor a house is unattended. Arrange for someone — a neighbor, a property-watch service, or a local contact — to physically check the house on a regular schedule through the winter: confirm heat is holding, look for water, collect mail, and make sure the place reads as looked-after even when it isn't lived in.

The part worth saying out loud

None of this is legal work. It's the maintenance an estate has to fund and coordinate to protect an asset that isn't anyone's home anymore but still belongs to the family until it sells. Skipping it doesn't save money — it just moves the cost from a manageable winter bill to a spring repair, right when the house needs to show well.

So the question worth asking before the first hard freeze: does this house have a plan for the next four months, or does it just have an address?

item.title: What You Sign Before You Tour: Buyer Agency in Montana
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Montana buyers now sign a written agreement before seeing the inside of a house. Here's what that document actually sets, and how to hold someone to it.
item.content:encoded:
What You Sign Before You Tour: Buyer Agency in Montana

Most buyers sign it on a doorstep. Phone in one hand, agent's tablet in the other, ninety seconds before the first showing of the day — and most of them don't read a line of it before they do.

That's the buyer representation agreement, and since the nationwide practice changes that followed the 2024 NAR settlement, it's not optional paperwork anymore. If you want an agent to walk you through a house that's listed with a Montana Regional MLS participant, you sign one first. So if you're about to start touring Kalispell or Whitefish homes and someone hands you a form before you've seen a single closet, here's what it actually says — and what to look at before your name goes on it.

The Document at the Door

A buyer representation agreement is a written contract between you and a real estate agent (or the agent's brokerage) that spells out the working relationship before any house-hunting starts. It's the buyer-side mirror of the listing agreement a seller signs with their agent. Neither is new in concept — what changed in 2024 is that it's now required in writing, signed, before a buyer's agent can tour a property with you.

That's a reasonable thing to require. A written scope of work is how you hold someone to a standard — what they're doing for you, how long, and on what terms. The problem isn't the requirement. The problem is signing it at the door without understanding what's in it.

Term and Exclusivity: What You're Actually Agreeing To

Two questions matter more than the rest of the page combined.

How long does it run? Some agreements run 90 days, some run a year. If this is your first time working with an agent, there's no reason to sign anything longer than a single showing or a short trial window — 30 days is common and reasonable to ask for. You can always extend it once you know the agent is a fit. Locking into a long term before the first tour is backwards.

Is it exclusive? An exclusive agreement means that agent represents you for the term, full stop — even if you stumble across a house on your own, at an open house, or through a friend's listing. A non-exclusive agreement lets you work with more than one agent at a time. Most buyers don't need multiple agents; they need to know which kind they signed. If you find a for-sale-by-owner or a new-construction spec home on a Sunday drive while under an exclusive agreement, that agent may still be owed a role — or a fee — depending on how the form is written. Ask before it happens, not after.

Scope and Compensation

The agreement also sets the territory: one specific property, a single town, or the whole Flathead Valley. If you're not sure yet whether you're buying in Kalispell proper or looking as far out as Columbia Falls or Bigfork, don't sign something that boxes you into one zip code before you've decided.

Then there's the part that changed the most in the last two years: how the agent gets paid, and who pays it. Buyer-agent compensation is no longer something that gets quietly handled through the MLS listing. The agreement states a specific number or percentage, and it states who's expected to pay it — the seller (through the offer), the buyer directly, or some combination negotiated deal by deal. None of that is fixed by law or by MLS rule anymore. It's a line in the document you're signing, and it's negotiable. Read it, and if the number doesn't match what you expected going in, ask about it before you're three showings deep.

The Protection Period

Most agreements include a protection period — a window, often 30 to 90 days after the agreement ends, during which the agent is still owed compensation if you buy a home they introduced you to or showed you during the term. This exists so an agent who does the work of showing you fifteen houses isn't cut out of the deal because you waited three weeks to make an offer. It's standard, and it's fair in principle. What matters is knowing the window exists and roughly how long it runs, so there's no surprise if you go back to a house you saw with one agent after you've started working with another.

If It Isn't Working

A buyer agreement isn't a life sentence. If the relationship isn't working — slow communication, a mismatch in how you search, an agent who isn't showing up prepared — most agreements have a cancellation path, and a good agent won't make you fight for it. Ask what that path looks like before you sign, not after you're frustrated. If it isn't spelled out, ask directly: "If this isn't a fit, how do we end it?" The answer to that question tells you a lot about who you're about to spend the next few months with.

None of this is a hurdle standing between you and the house you want. It's the tool that makes sure the person walking you through it is actually working for you, on terms you both agreed to and can both point back to. Read it before you sign it, ask the questions above, and the rest of the search gets a lot simpler.

item.title: Showings While You're Both Still Living There
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Neither of you has moved out yet, and the house is already listed. Here's how a showing schedule actually gets built — one calendar, confirmed appointments, and a plan for the kids — when two people who'd rather not coordinate directly still have to share a front door.
item.content:encoded:
Showings While You're Both Still Living There

The house is listed. Neither of you has moved out yet.

That's the month nobody plans for when a Flathead Valley divorce sale gets underway. Everyone braces for the closing table. Almost nobody braces for Tuesday at 4pm, when a buyer's agent wants to walk through the kitchen and both names on the deed are still sleeping under the same roof.

If you're wondering how other people get through this part without it becoming the worst month of the whole process, here's what actually works.

One calendar, not two phones

The single biggest mistake I see is treating showings like any other logistics question between two people who are separating — handled by text, in the moment, back and forth.

That works fine for deciding who picks up milk. It does not work for a stream of showing requests coming in from agents who don't know your situation and don't need to. Every request that lands in a group text becomes a small negotiation, and a house going through a divorce sale generates a lot of small negotiations before it generates a closing.

The fix is boring on purpose: one written calendar, one place, both of you can see it without asking the other person anything. I set this up before the sign goes in the yard, not after the first awkward showing. Requests come to me, I check it against the calendar, I confirm or propose an alternate time, and both of you get the same notice at the same time. Neither of you is coordinating with the other directly, and neither of you is finding out about a showing from a lockbox log.

Confirmed appointments only, and why that lowers the temperature

A house that's simply "available anytime" sounds convenient. In a situation like this, it's the opposite — it means either party can be caught off guard, which turns every doorbell into a small conflict.

Confirmed-appointments-only changes that. A showing isn't a showing until it's on the calendar and both parties have had the agreed notice window to prepare. No surprise walk-throughs, no "the agent said it would just be five minutes." That one rule removes most of the friction before it starts, because nobody is ever wondering whether someone might show up unannounced.

The kids' schedule sets the boundaries, not the buyer's

Buyers' schedules are flexible. A ten-year-old's school pickup is not. I build the showing windows around the school run and activities first, and everything else gets scheduled inside what's left — evenings after the bus, weekend blocks that don't collide with practices or the other parent's time. A buyer's agent asking for a Tuesday-at-3pm slot doesn't get to override that just because it's the only opening in their calendar; there's almost always another time that works, and it's my job to find it rather than yours.

Securing what shouldn't be part of the showing

A house that's occupied by two people mid-divorce usually has things sitting out that have nothing to do with selling it — financial documents, mail, medication, jewelry, anything either of you wouldn't want a stranger picking up off a dresser. Strangers walking through your home is already uncomfortable. It shouldn't also be a security risk.

Before the first showing, we walk the house together — or separately, whichever you prefer — and agree on where personal papers and valuables get secured for the duration of the listing. A lockable filing box in a closet, not spread across a desk. This is a five-minute conversation up front that saves a much worse one later.

Whose job it is to have the house ready

This is the question that causes the most friction, and it's worth answering explicitly rather than assuming. If one of you is home more, or one of you cares more about how the house shows, that's fine — but it should be agreed, not defaulted into. I put it in writing at listing: who's responsible for the house being presentable on a scheduled showing day, and what "presentable" means, so it isn't relitigated every week.

When one person starts declining showings

Sometimes a person who agreed to all of this at the start starts saying no to individual requests a few weeks in. Before assuming that's bad faith, it's worth asking why — a bad week, a scheduling conflict, or genuine discomfort with the pace. My job stays the same either way: keep both attorneys and both of you informed, document every request and every response in writing, and let that record speak for itself if it ever needs to. A documented process is a calm process, and staying neutral is what lets me keep working the file for both of you.

A question worth sitting with

If a buyer's agent called right now asking for a showing tomorrow at 5pm, would you know — without a single text to your ex — whether that works?

If the answer is no, that's the gap worth closing before the first showing request comes in, not after.

item.title: Ask Versus Close: What Flathead Sellers Are Actually Getting
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Every seller watches the list price. Almost none watch the gap between what a house asks and what it actually closes at — and right now in the Flathead, that gap is where the real story is.
item.content:encoded:
Every seller in the Flathead Valley can quote their neighbor's list price from memory. Almost nobody can tell you what that house actually closed at, or how many times the number changed between the sign going up and the sale going final.

That's backwards. The list price is a guess. The close price is the truth. And the spread between the two — plus how many times a seller had to move the ask to get there — is the single clearest read on where this market actually sits right now.

Numbers first, then what to do with them.

The Numbers: Mid-August Through Mid-September

For Kalispell, the period August 13 through September 13, 2026 (source: Montana Regional MLS data via IDEAL Real Estate's Kalispell market report, that period):

  • Active listings: 503, up 2.03% from the prior month
  • New listings: 104
  • Average asking price on active listings: $953,000 — down 10.24% from the prior month
  • Average original list price on that same pool: roughly $968,000
  • Price reductions: 141 listings, up sharply and now representing better than one in four active listings
  • Average days on market: 115.84 days, up 3.43%

Separately, Montana Regional MLS figures reported through Movoto put Kalispell's median closed sale price at $699,000 for August 2026, with median days on market at 77 — up from 62 days a year ago.

On rates: Freddie Mac's Primary Mortgage Market Survey put the 30-year fixed at 6.76% as of September 10, 2026, up slightly from 6.71% the week before.

A clean, published original-list-to-final-close ratio isn't available for this market this month — the MLS feeds that would produce it don't break it out publicly at the county level. But the two things that stand in for it, the reduction rate and the days-on-market trend, are telling the same story from two different directions, and it's worth reading them together instead of picking whichever one is more comfortable.

What the Reduction Rate Is Actually Telling You

More than one in four active Kalispell listings has already had at least one price cut. That's not a handful of overpriced outliers — that's a market-wide signal. When a quarter of the inventory needs a correction to keep moving, the problem isn't a few sellers who got greedy. It's that the starting assumption a lot of listings were priced against — where the market was a few months ago — has already moved on by the time the sign goes in the yard.

The average asking price on active listings has fallen roughly 10% in a single month, from an original average list closer to $968,000 down to $953,000 now showing. Some of that is new, more realistically priced inventory coming on. A meaningful piece of it is existing listings getting corrected because the first number didn't work.

Either way, the direction is the same: sellers are giving ground after listing, not before. That's the expensive way to find the right price.

Days on Market Is the Other Half of the Story

Average days on market sitting at 115.84 days — and separately, median days on market up to 77 from 62 a year ago — both point the same direction. Homes are taking longer to move than they were twelve months ago, and every extra week a listing sits is a week where a buyer sees the "days on market" counter climbing on the listing page and starts wondering what's wrong with the house rather than what's wrong with the price.

That's the mechanism worth understanding: a stale listing doesn't just wait for the right buyer. It actively signals something to every buyer who scrolls past it. By the time a seller finally cuts the price to where it should have started, they're often negotiating against their own listing history, not just the market.

What This Means If You're Pricing Right Now

If you're getting ready to list, the question isn't "what did the house down the street ask for." It's "what did the house down the street actually close at, and how many cuts did it take to get there." That number exists — your agent can pull it from sold comps — and it's a far better anchor than any asking price still sitting active on the market.

If you're already listed and haven't had a single showing in three weeks, the reduction-rate math above should tell you something: more than a quarter of your competition has already adjusted. Waiting to be the last one to move is not a strategy, it's a cost, measured in the extra days-on-market number that follows the listing around.

The sellers doing well in this market right now aren't the ones who priced highest. They're the ones who priced against where the market actually is today, took the showings that came in the first two weeks seriously as real feedback, and made one clean adjustment early instead of three small ones late.

If you're wondering whether your number is priced against last month's market or this one, that's worth a direct conversation before the listing goes live — not after it's been sitting for ten weeks.

item.title: The Plan You Hope You Never Open
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Every solid operation has a primary plan and a contingency, and the contingency gets written before anyone needs it. Here's how that habit applies to a real estate transaction — and why clients feel the difference when it does.
item.content:encoded:
Every transaction has two versions of what happens next. There's the one everybody's hoping for — clean appraisal, clean inspection, financing clears on schedule, keys change hands on the date printed on the contract. And there's the other one, the one nobody wants to talk about at the kitchen table: the appraisal comes in short, the buyer's financing falls apart with ten days left, the inspector finds something behind a wall nobody knew was there.

Most people only plan for the first version. That's backwards.

The Habit That Doesn't Come From Real Estate

Before any operation, there's a primary plan and there's a contingency — and the contingency doesn't get written in the middle of the crisis it's meant to solve. It gets written before anyone steps off, while everyone's calm and thinking clearly, precisely because that's the only time anyone thinks clearly. By the time something actually goes wrong, the plan already exists. Nobody's inventing a response under pressure. They're just executing the next page.

That habit doesn't turn off when the work changes. It shows up now in how a file gets prepared before a client ever asks a question, in how comps get run before they're needed rather than after, and in the fact that a contingency for the deal already exists before the deal needs one. It's not a personality quirk. It's a service standard — the same one that got applied under considerably higher stakes, just aimed at a closing table instead.

What "Having a Plan" Actually Looks Like in a Transaction

Talk to enough agents and you'll hear a lot of confidence and not much specificity. Confidence isn't the same as a plan. A plan has to answer real questions, in advance, before anyone's emotional about the answer:

If the appraisal comes in short — is the buyer prepared to bring the difference in cash, is the seller open to a partial price adjustment, or does the contract get renegotiated? That conversation should happen before an appraiser ever sets foot on the property, not after the number lands and everyone's scrambling.

If financing falls apart late — what's the buyer's backup lender, how fast can they actually move, and at what point does the seller need to know the listing might need to go back on the market? Ten days from closing is not when you want to be asking these questions for the first time.

If the inspection turns up something structural — is there already a sense of what repairs the seller will negotiate versus walk away from, and does the buyer have a number in mind for what changes the deal versus what they can live with? A pre-decided range keeps a hard conversation from turning into a stalled one.

If the buyer's own sale collapses — was there ever a contingency built around it in the first place, and if not, what's the fallback timeline everyone agreed to going in?

None of these are exotic. Every experienced agent has seen versions of all four. The difference isn't whether the scenario gets anticipated — it's whether it got discussed on a calm Tuesday afternoon or discovered on a panicked Thursday night with a closing date bearing down.

Why This Matters More Than It Sounds Like It Should

Here's the part that actually changes the client experience: when something does go sideways — and across enough transactions, something eventually does — the call that delivers the bad news is not the same call that leaves someone standing there with no idea what happens next. If the contingency was built ahead of time, that same phone call also delivers the next three steps. The client hears "here's what happened, and here's exactly what we do now" in the same breath.

Compare that to the alternative: the news lands, and now everyone's improvising a response to a problem that could have been anticipated a month earlier. That's where transactions actually fall apart — not usually because the underlying problem was unsolvable, but because nobody had a plan when it showed up, and improvised decisions under pressure are rarely anyone's best ones.

Panic, in a real estate transaction, is almost always a planning failure. It is not a personality failure, and it's not bad luck. It's a gap that existed before the stressful moment ever arrived, and it was closeable in advance.

What This Looks Like Working With Ryan

This isn't a pitch for pessimism, and it's not about assuming every deal is headed for trouble — most aren't. It's about treating a transaction the way any serious plan gets treated: build the primary path, and build the fallback before you need it, so that if the day comes, there's already an answer instead of a scramble.

Buyers and sellers in the Flathead Valley get that same approach applied to their file from day one — appraisal contingencies discussed up front, financing timelines built with slack instead of hope, inspection expectations set before the report ever arrives. Not because something is expected to go wrong, but because if it does, there's already a next step instead of a moment of silence on the phone.

If you're heading into a purchase or a sale and want to talk through what the contingency plan actually looks like for your situation — not the boilerplate version, the one built around your specific deal — that's a conversation worth having before you're under contract, not after.
